notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Joshua 23, drawn from the sources I could reach.

---

## Joshua 23 — Overview

The chapter is Joshua's farewell address to Israel's leaders, delivered about 25 years after the conquest when Joshua was around 110 years old. Commentators broadly agree that chapter 23 is a private meeting with tribal representatives (elders, heads, judges, officers), while chapter 24 is a more public covenant renewal gathering.

- **Donald Campbell** (cited at Precept Austin): "The Book of Joshua ends with the old soldier saying farewell. His parting addresses were tinged with sadness… They expressed the deep concern of Joshua who observed a growing complacency on the part of Israel toward the remnants of the Canaanites." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary
- **Don Anderson** (cited at Precept Austin): "The emphasis in chap. 23 is upon SEPARATION, and in chap. 24 on SERVICE." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary
- **David Guzik**: "Joshua could not, as a practical matter, speak to all Israel, so he spoke to the leaders… Joshua could reach all Israel by communicating well to the leaders." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/

---

### v. 1: "A long time after the LORD had given Israel rest from all the enemies around them, when Joshua was old and well along in years…"

- **Gill** says this was probably the last year of Joshua's life; the phrase "a long time" (literally "after many days," i.e., years) refers to the period after the land was divided and Israel had settled quietly. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Pulpit Commentary** notes that Joshua "waxed old and stricken in age" (literally "old, advanced in days") refers to a more advanced stage than Joshua 13:1; the patriarch now felt his powers failing and desired to preserve Israel in the right path. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joshua-23.html (search excerpt)
- **Precept Austin** notes that "rest" here means a peaceful situation free from external threat; it was a recurrent theme in Joshua (Josh 1:13; 11:23; 21:44; 22:4). Yet this rest did not mean all enemies were eradicated — Judges 3:2 says these enemies were left to test Israel. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) notes: "'Rest' is a common theme in Joshua; it was the goal of the Conquest. This rest was realized when the major battles were ended and Israel was settled in the land (Joshua 11:23). They were at peace with 'all their enemies' even though all those enemies had not yet been driven out." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/

---

### v. 2: "He summoned all Israel, including its elders, leaders, judges, and officers. 'I am old and well along in years,' he said."

- **Gill** explains that "all Israel" cannot mean the whole body of the people but the representatives: the seventy elders, the heads of tribes, the judges in their cities, and the officers who executed judgments. He also notes that Joshua's statement "I am old" was given "as a reason of his calling them together… and in order to command greater reverence of him." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **George Bush** (cited at Precept Austin) says the Hebrew indicates "called for all Israel, even for their elders," clearly showing the elders acted representatively. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary
- **Precept Austin** notes that unlike Caleb (who said he was "as strong today" as 45 years earlier), Joshua does not claim such strength — he simply acknowledges his advanced age. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary

---

### v. 3: "…you have seen everything that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, because it was the LORD your God who fought for you."

- **Ellicott** says Joshua here "speaks with characteristic modesty and humility." He begins by putting them in mind of divine interpositions, appealing to what their own eyes had seen, but so as "at once to abase himself and exalt the Most High. He does not say, 'Ye have seen what I have done… but what God himself has done.'" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/23.htm (search excerpt) and https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary
- **Guzik**: "Joshua began his address by giving glory to God. It would have been easy for Joshua to focus on what he had done as a military leader… But he was more interested in glorifying God than talking about himself." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Gill** points out that Joshua "does not attribute any of the things that were done to his own valour, nor theirs, nor so much as mentions himself or them as instruments, but wholly ascribes all to the Lord, who fought their battles for them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Precept Austin** notes that "because of you" (BSB "for your sake") is better understood as "on your behalf" — not because Israel deserved it, but all was the result of grace, based on divine fulfillment of covenant promises. "LORD your God" occurs 13 times in 9 verses in chapter 23; Joshua emphasizes Israel's covenant relationship with Yahweh. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary

---

### v. 4: "See, I have allotted as an inheritance to your tribes these remaining nations, including all the nations I have already cut off, from the Jordan westward to the Great Sea."

- **Gill**: "These nations that remain" refers to those yet unsubdued, and both the conquered and unconquered lands were divided by lot to the tribes. The inheritance "reached from Jordan eastward… to the Mediterranean sea, called the great sea in comparison of little ones in Canaan." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Precept Austin** (citing Bush): "I have divided unto you by lot. Heb. הפלתי לכם hippalti lâkem, I have caused to fall unto you." The "nations which remain" are the land/nations that remain unconquered — Joshua is reminding them that their inheritance is actually larger than what they currently occupied. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary
- **Guzik**: "Under Joshua's leadership, the army of Israel broke the back of the Canaanite military occupation. It remained for each individual tribe to fully possess what God gave to them." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/

---

### v. 5: "The LORD your God will push them out of your way and drive them out before you, so that you can take possession of their land, as the LORD your God promised you."

- **Gill** says this promise is "to be understood on condition of their good behaviour towards the Lord, and obedience to his commands; by which tenure they held the possession of the land when put into it, and for their disobedience did not possess the whole." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Guzik** adds a New Testament perspective: "God gives every believer an inheritance. In Jesus Christ, His people have been blessed… with every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3). God has a definite part for His people to play in coming to possess this inheritance." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Precept Austin**: "Note again Israel's responsibility in light of God's sovereignty" — God would do it, but through Israel's effort, faith, and courage. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary

---

### v. 6: "Be very strong, then, so that you can keep and obey all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, not turning aside from it to the right or to the left."

- **Ellicott**: "As Joshua was the servant of the law himself, so must his successors be. No higher position was attainable than this. It has been the same with the successors of the greater Joshua. With them, and with those who follow them, nothing can ever supersede the authority of the written word." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/23.htm
- **Guzik** (Pentecostal/charismatic): "Israel needed to be courageous, so they could be obedient. Obedience to God requires courage and sacrifice… They must not turn aside from it to the right hand or to the left, because there were dangerous extremes on either side. Either legalism or licentiousness among God's people pleases Satan." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Ligonier** (Reformed): "Obedience to the Lord in one generation does not guarantee obedience in the next… Every generation must be exhorted to continue following the Word of God (Ps. 78:5–8)." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/exhortation-to-faithfulness
- **Sam Storms** (charismatic): "A clear and unmistakable warning sign of impending abandonment of God is a diminishing respect for the authority of his Word. A disregard for biblical inspiration and authority is always the first step to spiritual rebellion." — https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/cling-to-the-lord-your-god-joshua-231-16
- **Gill**: keeping the law "required spiritual strength, fortitude of mind, a holy courage, a firm and fixed resolution, and particularly to destroy the Canaanites required in that book." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html

---

### v. 7: "So you are not to associate with these nations that remain among you. You must not call on the names of their gods or swear by them, and you must not serve them or bow down to them."

- **Ellicott**: "'Come not among these nations' — i.e., do not mix with them; literally, do not go in unto them. … It was a trial of Israel's faith and obedience to live among idolaters without making any peace with them, or lending any countenance to their idolatry." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/23.htm
- **Gill** is extensive here: "neither make mention of the name of their gods" means not even in common conversation, "and still less in any religious matters; never with any reverence of them… but always with indignation and contempt, calling them dunghill gods." On "nor cause to swear by them," Gill cites the Mishnah and Maimonides that even causing a Gentile to swear by an idol was forbidden. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Guzik**: "Joshua told Israel to not even make mention of the false gods of the Canaanites. Instead of learning about them or promoting them, they should hold fast to the LORD their God." Citing Hess: "This fundamental command against idolatry (Exodus 20:3–6; Deuteronomy 5:7–10) becomes the chief test of obedience." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/

---

### v. 8: "Instead, you shall hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day."

- **Sam Storms** (charismatic/Pentecostal): "The word translated 'cling' is the same as is translated 'hold fast' or 'cleave' in Genesis 2:24 where God says a man should leave his father and mother and 'cleave' to his wife. … To 'cling' to God is to stay so close to him that no sin can get between you." — https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/cling-to-the-lord-your-god-joshua-231-16
- **Guzik**: "Israel's greatest defense against apostasy would come by holding fast to the LORD, more than by understanding and refuting pagan worship. … The normal Christian, by and large, is not called to become an expert in the cults or in heresy, but to become an expert in Jesus Christ – to hold fast to Him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Gill** explains "as ye have done unto this day" refers to their conduct since entering Canaan under Joshua's government (not in the wilderness, where they frequently revolted). "This is to be understood not of individuals… but of the whole body, and with respect to any notorious offence, particularly idolatry." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Pulpit Commentary** (Homiletics): The duty is (1) Personal devotion — "God seeks the devotion of our hearts. It is inward and spiritual, and not merely a fact of visible conduct"; (2) Active obedience; (3) Purity. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/joshua/23.htm

---

### vv. 9–10: "The LORD has driven out great and powerful nations before you… One of you can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God fights for you, just as He promised."

- **Ellicott** notes the echo of Joshua 1:5 — "No man hath been able to stand before you." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/23.htm
- **Gill**: "Here Kimchi and Ben Melech observe, that the future tense is put for the past, and that the sense is, one of them had chased a thousand in their war with the Canaanites; but Abarbinel… thinks it refers to time to come, what they should be able to do if they cleaved unto the Lord; this was fulfilled in Samson, Judges 15:15; such a promise was made, Leviticus 26:8." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Guzik**: "As Israel was faithful and trusted in the LORD, they saw God do great things through them. As they continued to abide in Him, they would continue to see great things as God would fight on their behalf." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Precept Austin** (Utley): "God as warrior is a common theme of the Pentateuch (e.g., Dt. 1:30; 3:22; 20:4; Ex. 14:14) and Joshua… Notice, however, the previous phrase which emphasized the necessary cooperation of Israel ('because of you')." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-23-commentary

---

### v. 11: "Therefore watch yourselves carefully, that you love the LORD your God."

- **Morgan** (cited by Guzik): "Everything else is assured if men love Jehovah. Failure to keep the law is always the outcome of failure in love to the Lawgiver. For such failure in love, men are responsible. In order that love may be maintained, they need to take heed to themselves." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Guzik** (Pentecostal): "This call to love God was an appeal to the will. Believers must decide to love God, even if the feelings of love for Him don't come immediately." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Sam Storms**: "Note how often Joshua refers to God as 'your' God. No fewer than 12x… The emphasis here is on a relationship of intimacy: 'I am yours and you are mine!'" — https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/cling-to-the-lord-your-god-joshua-231-16
- **Gill**: "Take good heed therefore unto yourselves… to be upon their guard, and to be watchful, were very necessary to them, that they might not be ensnared by the Canaanites… that ye love the Lord your God; which would the most strongly influence and engage them to serve and worship the Lord." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html

---

### vv. 12–13: "For if you turn away and cling to the rest of these nations… intermarry and associate with them… they will become for you a snare and a trap, a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish…"

- **Ellicott**: "The common-sense of this warning is manifest. The God of Israel cannot treat as His enemies those whom Israel has united with itself, unless He also makes war on Israel. It was a long time before Israel learned the lesson how to live in the world without being of the world. It was not learnt until after the Babylonish captivity." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/23.htm
- **Guzik**: "What today seems like an 'innocent Canaanite' in the life of a believer may become a torture and a snare tomorrow. Such ungodly influences never advertise themselves as instruments of torture; they present themselves as wonderful additions." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Redpath** (cited by Guzik): "How often we see that the temptation we have pampered and encouraged and indulged in has become a scourge and a thorn in our side. The compromising Christian is not a happy man." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Trapp** (cited by Guzik): "As the fowler catcheth birds, and the hunter wild beasts in their snares and traps; so shall these Canaanites catch you by their familiarity and commerce, and draw you to participate in their sins and plagues." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Gill**: "they shall be snares and traps unto you; who by their bad examples would draw them both to idolatry and superstitious worship, and into all irreligion, profaneness, and immorality." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Ligonier** (Reformed): "Joshua focused on not adopting the ways of the Canaanites, not intermarrying with them and not joining them in their worship of false gods… As John Calvin comments, we must 'beware of allowing ourselves to become involved in fellowship with wickedness, by not keeping at a sufficient distance from it.'" — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/exhortation-to-faithfulness

---

### v. 14: "Now behold, today I am going the way of all the earth, and you know with all your heart and soul that not one of the good promises the LORD your God made to you has failed…"

- **Gill**: "Death is a journey from this world to another, a man's going to his long home, a path trodden by all men, and but once; a way in which all men without exception must and do walk, and even the best as well as the greatest of men, such as Joshua." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Ellicott**: "These words, as well as the similar statement in Joshua 21:43-45, show that though the conquest of Canaan by Joshua was in one way a limited conquest, yet it fully satisfied the hopes of Israel for the time: i.e., that they understood the Divine promises in that sense in which we see them to have been actually fulfilled." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/23.htm
- **Guzik**: "Joshua required that every man search his heart and see if there was ever a time when he could rightly accuse God of unfaithfulness." Citing Hess: "Joshua may die but God will not change. … Joshua repeats the fact that every word has come true. However, his purpose is not to praise God for his faithfulness but to warn Israel that God will apply this same faithfulness to his judgments upon the sinful nation." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Desiring God** (John Piper, Baptist/Reformed): In an article on God's faithfulness, Piper cites Joshua 23:14 as proof that "not one word had failed of all the good things that the Lord promised — all had come to pass." This is the foundation for trusting God's future promises. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/will-he-fail-me-now

---

### vv. 15–16: "But just as every good thing… has come to pass, likewise the LORD will bring upon you the calamity He has threatened… If you transgress the covenant… the anger of the LORD will burn against you, and you will quickly perish…"

- **Guzik**: "Joshua emphasized that God would be just as faithful to judge His disobedient people as He had been to bless His obedient people, according to the terms of Israel's covenant with God (Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 28)." He then adds a crucial New Covenant qualification: "God's people today relate to Him under a different covenant, a new and better covenant (Hebrews 8:6-7), by which Jesus Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:10-14). Therefore, in Jesus Christ, believers no longer experience God's faithfulness to curse as Israel knew it. Yet they do experience God's faithfulness to correct as a loving Father (Hebrews 12:7), and they will experience a lack of appropriated blessing if they do not abide in Jesus." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/
- **Gill**: "For as he is faithful to his promises, so to his threatenings; and from his punctual performance of the one may be argued and expected the sure fulfilment of the other, and which has been abundantly verified in that people." He cites the Babylonian captivity and the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans as fulfillments. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html
- **Ellicott** notes the resemblance to Deuteronomy 11:16-17: "Take heed to yourselves, lest… ye turn aside and serve other gods… and then the Lord's wrath be kindled against you… and ye perish quickly." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/23.htm
- **Trapp** (cited by Guzik): "To the sweetness of the promises he fitly adjoineth the tartness of the menaces. Sour and sweet make the best sauce: promises and threatenings mingled serve to keep the heart in the best temper." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed (Ligonier) Emphasis on Perseverance and Covenant

The Ligonier devotionals highlight that "the rest Joshua provided to Israel was only temporary. It would take a new and better Joshua — the Lord Jesus Christ — to bring full and final rest to God's people." The application is framed in terms of the perseverance of the saints: "We are called to continue in the faith so that we will enjoy that full rest in Christ's consummated kingdom (Heb. 3:7–4:13)." This reflects the Reformed concern with covenant faithfulness and perseverance as evidence of genuine faith. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/exhortation-to-faithfulness

### Charismatic/Pentecostal (Enduring Word / Sam Storms) Emphasis on the Will and Spiritual Warfare

Guzik (Enduring Word) frames loving God as "an appeal to the will. Believers must decide to love God, even if the feelings of love for Him don't come immediately." Sam Storms applies the "God fights for you" theme directly to spiritual warfare against Satan and demonic hosts (citing Ephesians 6:12), against the flesh, and against the world — a distinctively charismatic/Pentecostal paradigm. He also emphasizes that Joshua's warning concerns "the loss of earthly inheritance in the land," not "the loss of eternal life." — https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/cling-to-the-lord-your-god-joshua-231-16

### Baptist (Gill) Emphasis on the Law and Conditional Possession

Gill, writing as a Particular Baptist, stresses that the promise of verse 5 is conditional: "to be understood on condition of their good behaviour towards the Lord, and obedience to his commands; by which tenure they held the possession of the land." He also cites later rabbinic sources (Mishnah, Maimonides) for the prohibitions in verse 7, reflecting his extensive engagement with Jewish interpretive tradition. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-23.html

### Guzik's New Covenant Nuance (Pentecostal)

Guzik is careful to distinguish the Old Covenant pattern (blessing for obedience, curse for disobedience) from the believer's relationship under the New Covenant: believers are redeemed from the curse of the law (Gal 3:10-14), yet they experience God's fatherly correction (Heb 12:7) and can lack appropriated blessing if they fail to abide in Jesus. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-23/

---
